content.text: 9	We present the first systematic evaluation of safety commitment detection across four reasoning models spanning two architectures (Llama, Qwen), two training methods (R1 distillation, STILL), and two parameter scales (7--8B, 32B). Our central finding is methodological: the choice of layer selection metric entirely determines whether an HS advantage is observed. A natural composite metric (balanced accuracy $\times$ crossing rate) systematically selects shallow layers for 32B models because early layers produce more volatile representations that cross detection thresholds more frequently, inflating the crossing rate component independently of true discriminative power. At these biased layers, only 5 of 12 statistical tests survive Holm-Bonferroni correction, producing an apparent ``scale-dependent'' HS advantage that is significant at 7--8B but absent at 32B. A five-metric ablation reveals that four complementary metrics all converge on deep layers for every model (\cref{tab:layer_selection}). At these corrected layers, all 12 tests pass Holm-Bonferroni step-down correction ($\alpha{=}0.05$), with HS precision exceeding text by +15.4 to +23.6 percentage points (pp) across all four models (\cref{tab:hs_vs_text}). The layer selection metric, not scale or architecture, is the true moderator of probe performance. This result has implications beyond our specific task: any study that uses composite metrics to select probe layers risks the same systematic bias, and sensitivity analysis across multiple selection criteria should be standard practice in the probing literature.

This criterion does not affect step-level metrics (balanced accuracy, precision, FPR), which are computed over all steps independently. 52	\paragraph{Mechanistic explanation.} Shallow transformer layers produce more volatile representations across reasoning steps. This volatility causes probe scores derived from shallow layers to cross any fixed threshold more frequently, inflating the crossing rate component independently of whether the probe has learned genuinely informative features. The product metric therefore favors layers that are ``trigger-happy'' (high crossing rate due to representational instability) rather than layers whose representations encode the semantic distinction between pre-CP and post-CP states. The effect is strongest in deeper models: in 64-layer models (R1-32B, QwQ-32B), the biased metric selects layers at 3--16\% depth, while principled metrics converge on layers at 94--98\% depth.

68	\paragraph{Why deep layers are correct.} Our claim that deep layers provide the appropriate selection does not rest on the circular argument that ``HS probes outperform text probes at deep layers.'' Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion. First, the mechanistic analysis above identifies a specific, quantifiable bias in the crossing-rate metric that artificially inflates shallow-layer scores. Second, four of five selection metrics, each capturing a different aspect of probe quality, converge on deep layers. Third, the probing literature consistently finds that task-relevant semantic representations form in mid-to-deep transformer layers~\citep{belinkov2022probing, tenney2019bert}. The convergence of mechanistic reasoning, empirical metric agreement, and established probing theory provides a non-circular justification for deep-layer selection.

We present the first cross-model evaluation of temporal probing for safety commitment detection across four reasoning models spanning two architectures (Llama, Qwen), two training methods (R1 distillation, STILL), and two scales (7--8B, 32B). Our primary methodological finding is that layer selection methodology can reverse a study's conclusions: the composite metric \texttt{bal\_acc $\times$ crossing\_rate} systematically selects shallow layers at 32B scale, entirely masking the hidden-state advantage. At correctly selected layers, all 12 Holm-Bonferroni-corrected hypothesis tests confirm significant HS superiority, with precision gains of +15 to +24 percentage points (pp) across all four models ($n{=}19$--$47$ test traces; $n{=}19$--$20$ at 32B scale). Temporal windowing universally improves both modalities, providing the most robust single default for safety monitoring. Seven alternative approaches (change-point detection, geometric distance, Representation Engineering, CCS, nonlinear probes, cross-model transfer via PCA projection and direct application) all fail, establishing clear boundaries of current methods. Control tasks confirm genuine safety-specific structure (selectivity 7.5--18.3pp above chance).

\paragraph{Safety in Reasoning Models.}
Reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1~\cite{deepseekr1} and QwQ~\cite{qwq} introduce a qualitatively new safety failure: the model's own chain of thought can transition from safety-aware deliberation to harmful content generation without any adversarial input modification. \citet{harmthoughts} document this self-jailbreak phenomenon and provide step-level annotations of reasoning traces, establishing that commitment to harmful output emerges gradually across multiple reasoning steps. \citet{selfjailbreak} characterize the statistical properties of self-jailbreak, showing that longer reasoning chains increase circumvention probability, but do not propose a deployable detection mechanism. On the mitigation side, SafeThink~\cite{safethink} steers early reasoning steps toward safety through text-level CoT monitoring, while SafeRemind~\cite{saferemind} inserts entropy-triggered safety reminders into the reasoning stream. Both operate on generated text and assume that safety violations are linguistically explicit in the CoT. These works collectively characterize the problem or propose text-level interventions; none conducts a systematic modality comparison to determine whether hidden states or text better supports commitment detection.

\paragraph{Safety in Reasoning Models.}

H-CoT~\cite{hcot2025} demonstrates that reasoning chains can be externally hijacked to bypass safety constraints, complementing the self-jailbreak phenomenon where harmful transitions originate from the model's own deliberation. The reliability of reasoning traces is further complicated by unfaithful reasoning~\cite{chen2025unfaithful}, where models' stated reasoning does not reflect their actual decision process, motivating hidden-state monitoring that bypasses text entirely. On the mitigation side, SafeThink~\cite{safethink} steers early reasoning steps toward safety through text-level CoT monitoring, while SafeRemind~\cite{saferemind} inserts entropy-triggered safety reminders into the reasoning stream. \citet{ahrend2026safer_traces} measure and mitigate information leakage in reasoning traces, addressing a complementary safety dimension. Concurrent work traces refusal dynamics in standard language models~\cite{hu2026refusal_dynamics}; our work differs in focusing on the self-jailbreak commitment process specific to reasoning models, with an emphasis on the methodological finding that layer selection metrics can reverse probe-based conclusions. These works collectively characterize the problem or propose text-level interventions; none conducts a systematic modality comparison to determine whether hidden states or text better supports commitment detection.

\paragraph{Hidden-State Safety Detection.}
A parallel line of work uses internal model activations to detect safety violations. TrajGuard~\cite{trajguard} computes Mahalanobis distance from safe activation trajectories and achieves above 95\% defense rates on standard instruction-tuned LLMs. SafeSwitch~\cite{safeswitch} trains hidden-state classifiers that trigger safety interventions when activation patterns indicate harmful intent. SIREN~\cite{siren} monitors internal representations during generation and detects harmful content before it reaches users. These methods share a critical assumption: the threat originates from adversarial manipulation of the model's input (jailbreak prompts, adversarial suffixes). They operate at the token level and were evaluated against external attack vectors on instruction-tuned models that lack extended reasoning. The self-jailbreak setting differs fundamentally because the harmful transition is internal to the model's own deliberation rather than externally induced, and the relevant signal spans multiple reasoning steps rather than individual tokens. We reproduce TrajGuard in our setting (\cref{sec:negative}) and find that its geometric approach fails because discriminative signal for safety commitment resides in minor PCA components rather than the principal directions that dominate Mahalanobis distance computation.
tool_args.new_string:
\paragraph{Hidden-State Safety Detection.}
A parallel line of work uses internal model activations to detect safety violations. \citet{zhou2024alignment} show that safety-relevant information distributes across transformer layers in standard LLMs, with early layers already distinguishing malicious from benign inputs. The internal representation of safety is multi-dimensional: \citet{arditi2024refusal} identify a single refusal direction that mediates model safety behavior, while \citet{zhao2025harmfulness} show that harmfulness and refusal are encoded in separable directions, suggesting that text-level monitors may capture only the refusal signal while missing the harmfulness encoding. TrajGuard~\cite{trajguard} computes Mahalanobis distance from safe activation trajectories and achieves above 95\% defense rates on standard instruction-tuned LLMs. SafeSwitch~\cite{safeswitch} trains hidden-state classifiers that trigger safety interventions when activation patterns indicate harmful intent. SIREN~\cite{siren} monitors internal representations during generation and detects harmful content before it reaches users. SafeDream~\cite{safedream2026} proposes a proactive world model for early jailbreak detection, in contrast to passive probing approaches. These methods share a critical assumption: the threat originates from adversarial manipulation of the model's input (jailbreak prompts, adversarial suffixes). They operate at the token level and were evaluated against external attack vectors on instruction-tuned models that lack extended reasoning. The self-jailbreak setting differs fundamentally because the harmful transition is internal to the model's own deliberation rather than externally induced, and the relevant signal spans multiple reasoning steps rather than individual tokens. We reproduce TrajGuard in our setting (\cref{sec:negative}) and find that its geometric approach fails because discriminative signal for safety commitment resides in minor PCA components rather than the principal directions that dominate Mahalanobis distance computation.

\paragraph{Probing Methodology and Layer Selection.}
Linear probing is the standard tool for investigating what information transformer representations encode~\cite{belinkov2019analysis,hewitt2019control}. \citet{belinkov2019analysis} survey probing methods across NLP tasks and establish that task-specific representations form in different layers depending on the linguistic level of the target property. \citet{tenney2019bert} conduct layer-by-layer analysis showing that syntactic information concentrates in middle layers while semantic features emerge in deeper layers. \citet{hewitt2019control} introduce control tasks and selectivity metrics to distinguish genuine representational structure from probe memorization, a methodology we adopt to validate our safety probes (\cref{app:control}). Despite this methodological foundation, layer selection remains an underexamined researcher degree of freedom. Most probing studies select layers by a single validation metric and report results at that layer without sensitivity analysis. We demonstrate that this practice can reverse a study's central conclusion: a composite metric (balanced accuracy multiplied by crossing rate) systematically selects shallow layers for 32B models, producing qualitatively different findings than four alternative metrics that converge on deep layers (\cref{sec:layer-results}).

Despite this methodological foundation, layer selection remains an underexamined researcher degree of freedom. Most probing studies select layers by a single validation metric and report results at that layer without sensitivity analysis. 1	Large Language Models (LLMs) with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can self-jailbreak: their extended reasoning traces sometimes transition from safe deliberation to committed harmful generation. Detecting this \emph{safety commitment} in real time is essential for monitoring systems, yet no prior work has systematically compared hidden-state (HS) probes against text-based monitors for this task. We present the first cross-model evaluation of temporal probing for safety commitment detection across four reasoning models spanning two architectures (Llama, Qwen), two training methods (R1 distillation, STILL), and two scales (7--8B, 32B). Our primary methodological finding is that layer selection methodology can reverse a study's conclusions: the composite metric \texttt{bal\_acc $\times$ crossing\_rate} systematically selects shallow layers at 32B scale, entirely masking the hidden-state advantage. At correctly selected layers, all 12 Holm-Bonferroni-corrected hypothesis tests confirm significant HS superiority, with precision gains of +15 to +24 percentage points (pp) across all four models ($n{=}19$--$47$ test traces; $n{=}19$--$20$ at 32B scale). Temporal windowing universally improves both modalities, providing the most robust single default for safety monitoring. Seven alternative approaches (change-point detection, geometric distance, Representation Engineering, CCS, nonlinear probes, cross-model transfer via PCA projection and direct application) all fail, establishing clear boundaries of current methods. Control tasks confirm genuine safety-specific structure (selectivity 12.5--19.7pp above chance).

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We present the first controlled comparison of hidden-state and text-based probes for safety commitment detection in reasoning models, evaluated across four models spanning two architectures and two scales.
The central finding is methodological: a composite layer selection metric incorporating crossing rate reverses the study's main conclusion at 32B scale, while metrics from two measurement families (accuracy-based and false-positive-based) converge on deep layers where HS probes significantly outperform text probes on all four models (Holm-Bonferroni correction, 12 tests, $\alpha{=}0.05$; precision +15.4 to +23.6pp).
Future work should close the 85.5\% oracle gap through causal intervention techniques, extend to multilingual and multi-turn settings, and explore stronger cross-model alignment methods beyond PCA-based transfer.
